candidateRows: First-century Jewish concepts resembling incarnation and two divine powers supply the necessary framework for recognizing Jesus's claims to divine identity.
This establishes the historical-hermeneutical premise on which Wood's subsequent readings of Jesus's words, actions, and reception depend.
Wood argues that later Christian and Jewish developments obscured ideas once present within Judaism, causing modern readers to overlook claims intelligible to first-century audiences.
Old Testament portrayals of two distinguishable figures acting as Yahweh establish a two-powers framework in which Jesus identifies himself as one divine power.
This is Wood's principal explanation of how Jesus personally claims divine identity and supplies the conceptual framework for nearly all his textual examples.
Wood draws on paired Yahweh figures and the angel of the Lord to argue that Jewish scripture distinguished two divine agents, then says Jesus claimed to be one of them.
Jesus's identity should be inferred cumulatively from his words and deeds together with the words, deeds, and reactions of his followers and enemies.
The proposed cumulative method organizes the ensuing affirmative case and explains why hostile reactions and early Christian practices count as identity evidence.
After stating the two-powers thesis, Wood proposes examining what Jesus, his friends, and his enemies each say and do as a cumulative indication of Jesus's self-understanding.
Jesus identifies himself as the uniquely divine Son, David's heavenly Lord, and Daniel's cloud-riding Son of Man, thereby claiming to be one of two divine powers.
The passages are offered as direct evidence of Jesus's personal claims and therefore address the debate's central question rather than merely later Christian interpretation.
Wood connects sayings from Matthew and Mark with Psalm 110 and Daniel 7, arguing that Jesus assumes divine prerogatives and the identity of the heavenly Son of Man.
Jesus claims divine status by exercising Yahweh's roles as universal judge and raiser of the dead while requiring honor equal to the Father's.
The argument supplements titular claims with divine functions and equal honor, making Jesus's conduct and asserted authority independent support for divine identity.
Wood compares Old Testament descriptions of Yahweh's judgment and resurrection power with Jesus's claims in Matthew 25 and John 5 to perform those same functions.
The earliest Christians treated Jesus as the divine Lord and creative Word, gave him Yahweh's name and honors, and worshiped him as one of the two powers.
Early hymnic, Pauline, and Johannine material is used to corroborate Wood's account of Jesus's identity through the immediate beliefs and practices of his followers.
Wood invokes Philippians, Isaiah, First Corinthians, and John to argue that early believers applied divine names and honors to Jesus and incorporated him within Jewish monotheism.
In John 10 Jesus answers the accusation of claiming deity with Psalm 82, identifying his status with non-Yahweh beings called gods and clarifying that he is God's sent Son.
This directly contests whether a principal Johannine saying constitutes a personal claim to be Yahweh and supplies a delegated-status interpretation from Jesus's own response.
Wood's claim that Jesus's relationship to the Father places him within the Jewish two-powers framework.
O'Connor introduces Psalm 82's non-Yahweh gods and argues that Jesus cites it to correct his opponents' inference from unity with the Father to literal divine identity.
Johannine language about Jesus and the Father being one and mutually indwelling denotes a relationship believers may share, not identity between Jesus and Yahweh.
The argument targets central proof texts for divine identity and claims that their own parallels extend the same unity and indwelling to ordinary believers.
Wood's interpretation of Jesus's unity with and relation to the Father as evidence that Jesus is a divine heavenly power.
O'Connor compares John 10 with John 14 and John 17, emphasizing that disciples are promised the same oneness and mutual indwelling used to describe Jesus and the Father.
Jesus's 'I am' saying need not reproduce the Greek divine name, and even divine name-bearing can signify delegated authority rather than identity with Yahweh.
This addresses a prominent direct-identity proof text by combining a Greek lexical distinction with a Jewish agency framework in which representatives bear God's name.
The affirmative contention that Jesus's Johannine sayings and the angel-of-Yahweh tradition identify him personally as Yahweh.
O'Connor distinguishes the ordinary Greek expression used by Jesus from the Septuagint's divine-name wording, then turns to traditions in which non-Yahweh agents receive God's name and authority.
John 8:58 can identify Jesus as the eternally planned fulfillment of Abraham’s promised redemption without asserting Jesus’s personal preexistence or identity as Yahweh.
This supplies a direct alternative reading of a principal Johannine proof text and therefore bears centrally on whether Jesus personally claimed divine identity.
The affirmative interpretation of John 8:58 as Jesus claiming preexistence and divine identity.
After discussing divine name-bearing traditions, O'Connor connects the Abraham setting of John 8 with promised redemption and biblical language that treats predetermined events as already present.

The attempt to stone Jesus does not establish that his opponents correctly understood him as claiming to be God, because misunderstanding and broader accusations of blasphemy are recurring possibilities.
The move contests a major inference from hostile reactions to Jesus, weakening the claim that his enemies reliably confirm an intended assertion of deity.
The affirmative inference that attempted stoning for blasphemy confirms Jesus was understood correctly as claiming deity.
O'Connor argues that Johannine opponents repeatedly misunderstand Jesus and invokes Stephen’s prosecution to show that alleged attacks on law or custom could also attract blasphemy charges.

Jewish name-bearing traditions explain worshipful deference and divine authority without identifying the bearer as Yahweh, while Jesus also presents belief in himself as directed toward the one who sent him.
This articulates the critical side’s principal explanatory model for the debate: delegated divine name and authority rather than personal identity with Yahweh.
The affirmative claim that divine honors, titles, and authority attributed to Jesus identify him personally as Yahweh.
O'Connor uses a Josephus account of reverence toward a priest bearing the divine name, connects it to Jesus receiving the supreme name, and then stresses Jesus’s orientation toward his sender.

The scriptural distinction and interaction between Yahweh and the angel of Yahweh supports a two-powers framework in which Jesus claims to be the second heavenly power, not merely a delegated human representative.
The move restates and defends the affirmative’s overarching model of divine plurality against the critical side’s central name-bearing alternative.
O'Connor’s proposal that the angelic and christological material is adequately explained by delegated divine authority and name-bearing.
Wood compares Genesis accounts in which God commands Abraham and the angel speaks as the affected party, then contrasts Yahweh’s refusal to accompany Israel with the accompanying angel.
Jesus’s appeal to Psalm 82 is a legal defense against execution for using a divine title, not a retraction of his distinctive divine-son claim or an admission that he is merely an ordinary man.
This directly answers a key critical exegesis used to deny that Jesus intended the strong divine claim attributed to him in John’s Gospel.
O'Connor’s reading of Jesus’s Psalm 82 response as correcting the accusation that he had claimed equality with God.
Wood argues that Scripture’s application of divine terminology to others blocks an automatic blasphemy conviction but does not settle whether Jesus’s own greater title and claim are true.
Jesus’s claimed premundane glory, final judgment, and resurrection of the dead distinguish him from ordinary believers and assign him functions that the Old Testament reserves for Yahweh.
The argument combines preexistence with exclusive divine functions, providing affirmative evidence that exceeds a merely shared relationship or delegated human status.
O'Connor’s use of John 17 to argue that Jesus describes a relationship with God that can also be shared by believers.
Wood cites Jesus’s glory with the Father before creation and then contrasts general participation language with Jesus’s role as universal judge and the voice that raises the dead.
Stephen’s vision, prayer to Jesus, and the earliest Christians’ practice of calling on Jesus’s name show that Jesus was treated as a heavenly divine power within roughly two years of the crucifixion.
This offers early historical and textual evidence that Jesus occupied Yahweh’s devotional role, countering both delegated-authority and late-development explanations.
O'Connor’s appeal to Stephen as evidence that blasphemy and heavenly status do not require identifying Jesus as God.

Wood argues that violence begins specifically after Stephen sees Jesus as the Son of Man beside God, notes Stephen entrusts his spirit to Jesus, and connects Paul’s persecution to Christians invoking Jesus’s name.

Exodus’s statement that God’s name is in the angel fits divine name-bearing more naturally than a two-powers identity claim, while Jesus can remain an exalted and uniquely faithful servant rather than merely an ordinary man.
The move clarifies and defends the critical side’s main explanatory framework while rejecting Wood’s characterization of that position as reducing Jesus to an ordinary person.
Wood’s two-powers reading of the angel of Yahweh and his characterization of O'Connor’s Jesus as merely an ordinary man.

O'Connor cites the angel whose authority, capacity to forgive, and status derive from God’s name being in him, then describes Jesus as an ideal faithful servant occupying a special and exalted position.
Philippians 2 portrays Jesus as refusing to seize equality with God and receiving exaltation after obedient death, which fits an Adamic representative christology better than identity with Yahweh.
The argument supplies a major alternative reading of an early high-christology passage and challenges the inference that exalted status entails intrinsic equality with God.
Wood’s use of Philippians 2 as evidence for Jesus’s preexistent divine identity and equality with God.
O'Connor emphasizes that equality is not seized and that the supreme name is subsequently given, then contrasts Adam’s grasping with Jesus’s humility and resulting exaltation.

Jesus’s receipt and subsequent delegation of glory, judgment, and forgiveness shows that possession of supposedly divine prerogatives can reflect transmitted authority rather than personal identity as God.
This generalizes the critical side’s delegated-authority account across several of the affirmative’s principal categories of evidence for Jesus’s deity.
Wood’s argument that Jesus’s glory, universal judgment, and other divine functions identify him with Yahweh.

O'Connor observes that Jesus gives his received glory to disciples, promises them judicial authority, and authorizes them to forgive or retain sins, while still affirming Jesus’s special relationship with God.
The Gospel portrayal of deliberate obscurity and the Synoptic messianic secret undermines the claim that Jesus clearly communicated a public claim to be God.
The move challenges whether an explicit divine-identity claim is the best explanation of the textual record by appealing to pervasive misunderstanding and concealed identity.
David's contention that denying a divine claim would make Jesus an implausibly poor communicator.
After discussing the Greek wording of Lord, Alex argues that disciples and opponents misunderstood Jesus and contrasts Johannine divine-name readings with the Synoptic secrecy motif.
Jesus is better understood as an ideal human exercising God-given powers, because comparable powers and privileges are also extended to disciples and other humans.
This supplies the critical side's principal alternative explanation for deeds and prerogatives that the affirmative treats as evidence of divine identity.
David's inference that uniquely divine acts and prerogatives performed by Jesus establish Jesus's divine identity.
Alex uses Peter walking on water, disciples forgiving sins and judging Israel, shared unity, and shared glory to argue that such features can be delegated rather than ontological.
Jesus accepting proskynesis does not establish divinity, because the term commonly denotes bodily homage to human authorities while exclusive cultic service is expressed differently.
The distinction directly contests a major affirmative evidence class by arguing that the Gospel language for homage does not itself denote worship reserved exclusively for God.
David's appeal to Gospel passages in which Jesus accepts worship as evidence that Jesus is God.
Alex contrasts proskynesis with latreuo, lists humans and angels receiving the former, and notes sparse or contested Gospel instances of Jesus receiving such homage.
The converging testimony of Jesus's deeds, followers, enemies, blasphemy accusations, and two-powers imagery is best explained by Jesus claiming to be God.
This is an explicit cumulative case for the affirmative interpretation and directly states why divine self-identification best explains the debate's central textual phenomena.
Alex's proposed explanation of the evidence through delegated authority, ideal humanity, and divine name-bearing.
David combines judgment, resurrection, prayer and worship by followers, accusations by opponents, and deaths for related claims, then illustrates the convergence with an analogy.
The divine-name-bearing and ideal-servant interpretations fail because the Exodus messenger is identified with Yahweh and a merely ideal servant should not receive prayer and religious worship.
The move attacks the critical side's two principal alternatives and defends the religious significance of worship as evidence that Jesus is more than a human representative.
Alex's claims that Jesus bears God's name as a representative and is portrayed as God's ideal human servant.
David argues that Yahweh identifies himself with the guiding angel, calls worship and prayer unsuitable for a mere servant, and distinguishes religious proskynesis from ordinary respect.
Philippians 2 depicts a preexistent divine being who voluntarily assumes human likeness, not an ordinary image-bearing human who is only later elevated.
The passage supplies direct support for preexistence and divine status while rebutting an important later-exaltation reading offered by the critical side.
Alex's interpretation of Philippians 2 as an ideal human refusing grasped equality and subsequently receiving exaltation.
David argues that self-humbling precedes being made in human likeness and that universal homage and Isaiah's exclusive Yahweh language cannot naturally confer mere created status.
Jesus's use of the Septuagint's doubled Kyrios formula and the shared conclusion of followers and enemies support an intentionally veiled but genuine divine claim.
This defends a specific divine-name argument and converts the alleged ambiguity of Jesus's speech into a cumulative inference from the reactions surrounding him.
Alex's arguments that the Septuagint wording is ordinary Lord language and that Jesus's identity was intentionally unclear.
David says the doubled Greek title points specifically to Yahweh, grants gradual and careful disclosure, and argues that common divine readings by friends and enemies require explanation.
The New Testament's distribution and manuscript history of proskynesis, together with its absence of latreuo directed to Jesus, undercut worship as evidence of Jesus's deity.
The extended move systematically answers the affirmative worship case using lexical distinctions, textual criticism, cross-Gospel patterns, and Septuagint usage.
David's claim that proskynesis in a religious context is worship and that Jesus's receipt of it indicates divine identity.
Alex surveys Mark, Luke, John, Matthew, early manuscript variants, many nondivine recipients of proskynesis, the temptation narrative, and the exclusive association of latreuo with God.
Jesus's prayer before raising Lazarus shows that his miraculous authority is received from and exercised in continuing communication with the Father rather than independently possessed.
The argument directly uses a prominent miracle to support delegated agency, challenging the inference from Jesus's apparent command over life to intrinsic deity.
The affirmative claim that Jesus raises the dead on his own authority and thereby displays a prerogative belonging to God.
Alex compares Jesus with prophetic raisings, cites Jesus thanking the Father before calling Lazarus out, and generalizes that apparently independent miracles follow divine communication.
Jesus's Sabbath conduct need not identify him as God, because Mark grounds Sabbath liberty in David's precedent and humanity's priority over the Sabbath.
The move contests a major Johannine divine-identity inference by supplying a Synoptic parallel in which Sabbath authority is explained through human precedent and purpose.
David's reading of John 5 in which Jesus works on the Sabbath because he shares God's unique continuing work.
Alex appeals to David eating sacred bread, the Sabbath being made for humanity, disputed senses of Son of Man, and early interpretation to challenge an exclusively divine privilege.
John 5 permits delegated-authority readings and does not unambiguously present Jesus as claiming divine identity.
This challenges a principal Johannine text offered for Jesus personally claiming equality with God and supplies a competing interpretation.
Wood's claim that Jesus working because the Father works cannot describe merely human status.
After Wood distinguishes John 5 from the Markan Sabbath episode, O'Connor argues that the language may indicate permission or shared Sabbath liberty rather than identity with God.
The full sequence in John 5 attributes divine works and equal honor to the Son, making a merely delegated or ordinary-human reading inadequate.
The move presents a cumulative textual case that Jesus exercises life-giving and final-judgment functions associated with divine identity.
O'Connor's alternative interpretation of Jesus working on the Sabbath and his comparison with Mark.
Wood answers by tracing John 5 from the persecution narrative through equal honor, raising the dead, possessing life, and judging, treating the sequence as one integrated claim.
John 5 repeatedly says the Son's life and judicial authority are granted or entrusted, which indicates dependence on the Father rather than necessary divine possession.
This directly advances the delegated-authority alternative in the motion by grounding the distinction between Father and Son in the passage's own verbs.
Wood's cumulative reading of John 5 as assigning intrinsically divine life-giving and judgment to Jesus.
O'Connor examines the wording of John 5 and argues that judgment, life, and resurrection authority flow from the Father to the Son rather than belonging to the Son necessarily.
Receiving authority is compatible with prior divine identity because the Son becomes a servant in incarnation and is subsequently exalted in Daniel 7, Philippians 2, John 1, and Matthew.
The move supplies the affirmative's central reconciliation of Jesus receiving authority from the Father while nevertheless sharing divine identity.
O'Connor's argument that receiving life and authority from the Father is incompatible with Jesus being God.
Wood argues that the cloud-riding Son of Man is divine yet receives dominion, and that incarnation explains why one divine in nature lives as a servant before exaltation.

If Daniel 7 plainly identifies the Son of Man as Yahweh, the Sanhedrin should already have expected a divine Son of Man, making their reaction at Jesus's trial difficult to explain as a novel divine claim.
This tests the historical plausibility of using the trial reaction to establish that Jesus deliberately identified himself as Yahweh through Daniel 7.
Wood's claim that cloud-riding in Daniel 7 identifies the Son of Man as Yahweh.
O'Connor argues that a straightforward divine reading should have been embedded in Jewish expectation before the trial, rather than becoming apparent only when Jesus applied the text to himself.

Daniel 7's combination of cloud-riding, universal worship, and everlasting dominion naturally depicts a divine figure, while the separate Ancient of Days explains the history of interpretive confusion.
The move defends the textual foundation for the two-divine-figures reading on which the affirmative interpretation of Jesus's Son of Man claim depends.
O'Connor's challenge that Jewish readers should already have expected the Danielic Son of Man to be Yahweh.
Wood concedes diverse interpretations but contends that cloud-riding, worship by all nations, and eternal kingship point to deity, with the Ancient of Days creating the apparent two-powers mystery.
The blasphemy charge cannot establish Jesus's divine identity without independently showing that the high priest interpreted Daniel 7's Son of Man as Yahweh rather than as Messiah or Israel.
This identifies a potential circularity in a principal affirmative inference from the high priest's reaction to Jesus's intended personal claim.
Wood's use of the high priest's blasphemy accusation to confirm a Yahweh-identifying reading of Daniel 7.
O'Connor argues that messianic and corporate-Israel readings existed, and that Wood must establish the high priest's specific Yahweh reading before treating the death verdict as confirmation.
The lack of early literary traces of a two-powers controversy undermines the claim that this interpretation was sufficiently established to govern the high priest's reaction to Jesus.
The historical dating challenge bears directly on whether a two-powers framework can explain the trial scene and Jesus's intended meaning in its original setting.
Wood's claim that first-century readers were already confronting a widespread two-powers-in-heaven issue.
The exchange turns from textual interpretation to historical attestation, with O'Connor challenging the proposed popularity and antiquity of the two-powers framework through a scholarly source.
Jesus's words, deeds, followers, and enemies converge on a two-powers divine claim, and its very early reception rules out both late legend and universal misunderstanding.
This is the affirmative's concluding synthesis connecting Old Testament divine plurality, Jesus's prerogatives, earliest Christian practice, and hostile reactions.
O'Connor's delegated-authority readings, historical dating objections, and suggestion that divine identity is not the necessary interpretation.

Wood closes by connecting two-powers patterns across scripture with Jesus judging and raising the dead, early worship and prayer to Jesus, hostile reactions, and the rejection of legend or wholesale misunderstanding.
Jesus extends unity, glory, forgiveness, and judgment to disciples in the same pattern by which he receives them from the Father, favoring delegated authority over exclusive divine identity.
This concluding synthesis directly supports the critical side of the motion by arguing that allegedly divine prerogatives are transferable rather than unique identifiers of deity.
Wood's reliance on Jesus's unity with the Father and exercise of divine prerogatives as indicators of personal divine identity.
O'Connor closes by combining John 17's shared unity with the transfer of glory, forgiveness, mission, and judgment, while also renewing the objection to early dating of two-powers controversy.
Theosis resolves the delegation problem only if Jesus understands his own relation to the Father as the same kind of derived participation in divinity.
The answer preserves Alex's central delegated-authority account against a proposed orthodox explanation for disciples sharing divine prerogatives.
The moderator's proposal that orthodox theosis explains why a divine Jesus can share divine authority with disciples.
After Alex argues that Jesus passes glory, forgiveness, and judgment to followers, the moderator asks whether Eastern Orthodox deification dissolves that objection.
Hebrews probably presents a high christology and offers a strong challenge to Alex's earlier objection to identifying the angel of Yahweh with Jesus.
The concession materially qualifies the critical case by accepting early high christology in Hebrews while leaving the historical self-claim question open.
The audience argument that Hebrews depicts Moses enduring disgrace for Christ, implying Christ's activity before the incarnation.
An audience member cites Hebrews 11 to challenge Alex's claim that an inactive preexistent Jesus sits awkwardly with Hebrews' account of earlier revelation.

The Synoptics omit Johannine-style sayings because the Gospel authors emphasize different material, while Mark still progressively discloses Jesus's divine identity and Paul proves high christology was early.
This directly answers a major source-critical objection to relying on John and argues that divine christology is neither uniquely Johannine nor necessarily late.
The audience objection that Jesus's strongest Johannine divine declarations are absent from Mark, Q, Matthew, and Luke.
Asked why the earliest Gospel sources lack John's powerful divine declarations, David appeals to distinct authorial emphases and early non-Johannine christology.
The meaning of Philippians 2 may remain disputed, but even granting Paul a high christology does not establish that Jesus personally claimed to be God.
Alex separates later or Pauline beliefs about Jesus from the debate's historical proposition concerning Jesus's own claims, protecting his core case from a concession.
The audience request that Alex justify his preferred rendering of morphe in the Philippians 2 Christ hymn.
In response to a lexical question about morphe, Alex acknowledges interpretive uncertainty and explains that Pauline christology is secondary to Jesus's self-understanding.
In Philippians 2, being in the form of God naturally conveys being divine in nature, whereas Dunn's image-of-God reading fails to fit the passage.
The lexical interpretation supports the affirmative claim that an early Christian text depicts Jesus as divine before taking servant form.
Alex's appeal to James Dunn's interpretation and the audience question about whether morphe means form or divine nature.
After Alex declines a firm lexical preference, David explains why a meaning-based translation such as divine nature is appropriate in this context.
The use of morphe for Jesus appearing in a different outward form in Mark undermines the claim that the word itself must denote divine essence in Philippians.
This supplies a concrete counterexample to the affirmative lexical inference from form of God to possession of God's essential nature.
David's claim that morphe in Philippians naturally communicates divine nature and that Dunn's alternative makes no sense.
Alex responds to David's reading by comparing another occurrence of morphe, arguing that the term can refer to changed appearance rather than essence.
A changed human appearance is intelligible as a different form, but being in the form of God requires a deeper explanation consistent with divine nature.
The distinction attempts to neutralize Alex's lexical counterexample and preserve Philippians 2 as evidence of preexistent divinity.
Alex's argument that Mark's use of morphe for a different appearance shows the word need not indicate essential nature.
David distinguishes an ordinary change of visible human form from the unusual claim that someone exists in God's form, which he treats as ontologically weightier.
On Dunn's reading, form of God means bearing God's image, so that sense remains consistent with morphe also describing a different visible appearance.
This defends a non-ontological interpretation of Philippians 2 against David's claim that only divine nature makes sense of the phrase.
David's contention that being in God's form cannot be explained like an ordinary change in appearance and therefore implies divine nature.
Alex clarifies that Dunn connects divine form with humanity's creation in God's image and argues that this does not conflict with appearance language elsewhere.
Dunn's interpretation fails because Philippians contrasts Christ's initial divine form with his subsequent assumption of servant and human form.
The proposed sequence of divine form followed by servant form reinforces the affirmative appeal to preexistence and incarnation in an early text.
Alex's defense of Dunn's image-of-God interpretation as consistent with both Philippians and Mark's appearance usage.
David shifts from the isolated word to the hymn's sequence, arguing that taking servant form presupposes an earlier divine form from which Christ descends.
